questions.title: Method Call and Return Value Capture
questions.question: Declare a static method that computes and returns an `int` result, invoke it from `main`, capture the returned value in a local variable, and print it[cite: 9, 11].
questions.explanation: In Java, non-void methods return a typed value to their invocation call site via the `return` statement[cite: 9]. When `computeSquare(int n)` executes, the JVM allocates a call frame on the execution stack, performs the multiplication, pushes the resulting primitive `int` onto the operand stack, and transfers control back to the caller frame via the `ireturn` instruction[cite: 7, 9]. The caller assigns this operand to a local variable slot (`int result = computeSquare(10);`)[cite: 1, 9]. Capturing return values allows computed data to flow deterministically across method boundaries without mutating global or shared object state[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Declare the method with an explicit `public static int` return type signature[cite: 9].
Use the assignment operator `=` at the call site to store the returned primitive in a variable[cite: 7].
Print the captured local variable to standard output with descriptive labeling[cite: 1].

questions.title: Void Return Semantics and Incompatibility
questions.question: Invoke a `void` method, observe its side-effect output, and document via comments why attempting to assign a `void` method call to a variable causes a compile-time error[cite: 9, 11].
questions.explanation: A method declared with the `void` return keyword indicates to the Java compiler that the method produces no result value upon completion[cite: 9]. In the generated bytecode, a void method finishes with a plain `return` instruction that leaves the operand stack empty[cite: 9]. Because `void` is an uninstantiable pseudo-type rather than a data type, the expression does not evaluate to any runtime value[cite: 9]. Attempting to assign the outcome of a void invocation (such as `int x = logMessage();`) results in javac throwing an 'incompatible types: void cannot be converted to int' error[cite: 5, 9]. Void methods are used exclusively for procedural operations and side effects, such as writing to standard output or updating instance state[cite: 9, 10].
hints: Declare the helper method using `public static void`[cite: 9].
Invoke the method as an independent statement without an assignment operator[cite: 9].
Add a header or inline comment detailing why `int x = logMessage();` fails compilation[cite: 1, 9].
questions.expectedOutput:
Log: Method called successfully
Returned value: void (no value produced)

questions.title: Direct Chained Method Invocation
questions.question: Write a method that returns a `String` reference, and chain the `.toUpperCase()` invocation directly onto the method call without using an intermediate local variable[cite: 11].
questions.explanation: In Java's expression grammar, method invocations that return reference types evaluate directly to object references on the JVM operand stack[cite: 9]. Because `getLanguageName()` returns a `java.lang.String` reference, the member access operator (`.`) can be appended immediately to the call: `getLanguageName().toUpperCase()`[cite: 9]. The JVM invokes `getLanguageName()`, pushes the returned heap address onto the operand stack, and immediately invokes `toUpperCase()` on that reference via `invokevirtual`[cite: 9, 10]. Direct chaining eliminates boilerplate intermediate variables for transient operations, though developers must ensure the called method never returns `null` to avoid an immediate `NullPointerException`[cite: 5, 7].
hints: Implement `public static String getLanguageName()` that returns a non-null string literal[cite: 9].
Append `.toUpperCase()` directly to the invocation expression[cite: 11].
Print the chained expression result directly inside `System.out.println`[cite: 1].

questions.title: Deterministic Parameterized Invocations
questions.question: Call a pure mathematical method multiple times with distinct arguments, displaying how the return values differ deterministically based on input parameters[cite: 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Methods encapsulate parameterized algorithms whose output depends strictly on the input arguments passed to their parameters[cite: 9]. Each time `cube(int n)` is called, a new stack frame is pushed onto the thread stack, initialized with the passed integer value in local variable slot 0[cite: 1, 9]. When `cube(2)` is evaluated, the method calculates $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ and returns[cite: 9]; when `cube(3)` is evaluated, an independent call frame calculates $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ and returns[cite: 9]. Calling a pure method repeatedly with different arguments demonstrates referential transparency and algorithmic determinism without leaking state between invocations[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Write `public static int cube(int n)` returning `n * n * n`[cite: 9].
Invoke `cube()` sequentially using arguments such as 2, 3, and 4[cite: 9].
Print each invocation along with its corresponding evaluated result[cite: 1].

questions.title: Nested Method Call Evaluation Hierarchy
questions.question: Implement arithmetic helper methods and demonstrate nested method evaluation by executing `print(add(multiply(2, 3), 4))`[cite: 11].
questions.explanation: Nested method calls adhere to Java's strict inside-out operand evaluation order (JLS §15.7)[cite: 7]. In the expression `add(multiply(2, 3), 4)`, the JVM must evaluate all arguments before invoking the outer method[cite: 9]. First, `multiply(2, 3)` executes, returning 6 onto the operand stack[cite: 9]. Next, the literal 4 is loaded, and `add(6, 4)` executes, returning 10[cite: 9]. Finally, this resulting integer is passed as the parameter to `System.out.println`[cite: 1]. Each nested call pushes and pops its own isolated stack frame in last-in, first-out (LIFO) order, illustrating hierarchical expression composition[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Implement `public static int multiply(int a, int b)` returning `a * b`[cite: 9].
Implement `public static int add(int a, int b)` returning `a + b`[cite: 9].
Pass the call to `multiply` as the first argument of `add`[cite: 11].

questions.title: Predicate Method in Conditional Control Flow
questions.question: Write a boolean predicate method `isValidScore(int score)` and invoke it directly within an `if-else` branching condition[cite: 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Because conditional statements (`if`, `while`) require an expression that evaluates to a primitive `boolean`, a method returning `boolean` can be placed directly inside the conditional expression without explicit equality comparisons[cite: 7, 9]. Writing `if (isValidScore(score))` is more idiomatic than writing `if (isValidScore(score) == true)`[cite: 7, 9]. At the bytecode level, the method invocation pushes an integer 1 (`true`) or 0 (`false`) onto the stack, which the subsequent `ifeq` branching instruction consumes to direct execution to either the `if` body or the `else` branch[cite: 7, 9]. Encapsulating complex boundary checks into named predicate methods improves domain clarity and reduces logical bugs[cite: 9].
hints: Define `public static boolean isValidScore(int score)` returning `score >= 0 && score <= 100`[cite: 7, 9].
Place `isValidScore(score)` directly inside the `if` parentheses[cite: 9].
Test with representative values to verify both true and false branching paths[cite: 7].
questions.expectedOutput:
Method called successfully
Returned value: Valid score approved

questions.title: Primitive Array Compound Return
questions.question: Implement a method that calculates both the quotient and remainder of two numbers and returns both results packed into a two-element `int[]` array[cite: 7, 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Under the Java Language Specification, methods can return at most one value or reference type[cite: 9]. When an algorithm produces multiple interrelated results (such as integer division producing both a quotient and a remainder), packing them into a container object allows compound data to be returned via a single reference[cite: 7, 9]. Inside `divideWithRemainder(int dividend, int divisor)`, the method allocates a new array on the heap (`new int[]{dividend / divisor, dividend % divisor}`) and returns its memory pointer[cite: 5, 7, 9]. The caller receives the array reference and accesses individual components by zero-based index, maintaining structural cohesion without relying on global state[cite: 1, 3, 6].
hints: Specify the return type as `int[]` in the method declaration[cite: 9].
Construct and populate the array using `new int[]{dividend / divisor, dividend % divisor}`[cite: 7, 9].
Access the quotient via index 0 and remainder via index 1 at the call site[cite: 1, 3].

questions.title: Class-Encapsulated Compound Return Value
questions.question: Create an immutable `Coordinate` holder class with `x` and `y` fields, and write a method that computes and returns an instance of it[cite: 6, 9, 11].
questions.explanation: While returning an array allows grouping values of the same type, arrays lack named fields and type safety when combining heterogeneous data[cite: 9]. Creating a dedicated holder class or record provides self-documenting, type-safe compound returns[cite: 4, 9]. The `Coordinate` class declares `public final int x;` and `public final int y;` fields assigned in its constructor[cite: 6, 10]. A translation method `translate(Coordinate p, int dx, int dy)` instantiates and returns a new `Coordinate(p.x + dx, p.y + dy)`[cite: 6]. This pattern encapsulates related fields into a single domain abstraction, preventing index confusion bugs common with array-based multi-value returns[cite: 9].
hints: Define a class or record `Coordinate` with final fields `x` and `y`[cite: 4, 6].
Instantiate the object using `new Coordinate(...)` within the helper method[cite: 6, 9].
Access the returned values via named accessors or fields rather than array indices[cite: 4, 9].

questions.title: Fluent Method Chaining with 'this' Reference
questions.question: Implement a `MessageBuilder` class whose mutator methods return `this`, allowing calls to be chained together fluently[cite: 6, 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Method chaining (the fluent builder pattern) is an object-oriented idiom where mutator methods return the reference to the current object (`return this;`) rather than `void`[cite: 6, 9, 10]. When a method returns `this`, the caller receives the heap reference of the active instance, enabling another method to be called immediately on that same instance: `builder.setRecipient(...).setContent(...).build()`[cite: 6, 9]. This removes the need to repeat the variable name on each line, producing clean, readable code commonly used in domain-specific builders, stream configurations, and query generators[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Declare each builder mutator with the class type as its return type (e.g., `public MessageBuilder setSender(...)`)[cite: 6, 9].
Conclude every chaining method with `return this;` to return the active instance[cite: 6, 9].
Provide a terminal `.build()` or `toString()` method that outputs the configured state[cite: 9].
questions.expectedOutput:
Method called successfully
Result: To: Akshat | Body: Welcome to Advanced Java

questions.title: Static vs Virtual Method Dispatch
questions.question: Demonstrate the operational difference between calling a `static` method via class qualification and calling an instance method on an instantiated object of another class[cite: 1, 6, 9, 11].
questions.explanation: The JVM distinguishes between static and instance methods using different bytecode instructions[cite: 1, 9]. Static methods belong to the class definition in Metaspace and are invoked via `invokestatic ClassName.methodName()` without requiring an object on the heap[cite: 1, 6, 9]. Static calls are bound statically at compile time[cite: 9]. Instance methods, by contrast, require a live object instance on the heap and are invoked via `invokevirtual objRef.methodName()`[cite: 1, 5, 9, 10]. Virtual dispatch performs runtime dynamic method lookup, passing the object reference as an implicit first parameter (`this`) in local variable slot 0 of the callee's stack frame[cite: 6, 9, 10].
hints: Invoke the static utility method directly using `ClassIdentifier.staticMethodName()`[cite: 1, 9].
Use `new OtherClass()` to allocate an instance on the heap before invoking its instance method[cite: 1, 5, 6].
Compare the two call sites to illustrate class-scoped versus instance-scoped dispatch[cite: 6, 9].

questions.title: Optional Return Type for Missing Values
questions.question: Implement `findFirstNegative(int[] arr)` returning `java.util.Optional<Integer>` to represent absent results safely without returning `null`[cite: 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Returning `null` to indicate the absence of a result is a common source of unexpected `NullPointerException`s in Java applications[cite: 5, 7]. Introduced in Java 8, `java.util.Optional<T>` provides a type-level wrapper that explicitly indicates whether a non-null return value is present[cite: 9]. If `findFirstNegative` encounters a negative integer, it wraps the value in `Optional.of(n)`[cite: 9]; if no negative numbers exist or the array is empty, it returns `Optional.empty()`[cite: 9]. Callers handle the result using functional methods like `.ifPresentOrElse()`, `.orElse()`, or `.isPresent()`, forcing developers to handle empty cases explicitly at compile time[cite: 9].
hints: Declare the return type as `Optional<Integer>` in the method signature[cite: 9].
Return `Optional.of(num)` when a negative value is found[cite: 9].
Return `Optional.empty()` if the loop finishes without finding any negative elements[cite: 9].

questions.title: Multi-Branch Early Return Guard Clauses
questions.question: Implement `classifyScore(int score)` using early `return` guard clauses to map integer scores to academic grades, validating preconditions and avoiding nested `if-else` blocks[cite: 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Deeply nested `if-else` chains (the 'arrow anti-pattern') increase code complexity and make execution paths harder to trace[cite: 9]. The early return pattern uses guard clauses at the beginning of a method to handle edge cases and boundary conditions upfront[cite: 9]. If `score < 0 || score > 100`, `classifyScore` throws an `IllegalArgumentException` or returns an error status immediately[cite: 9]. Subsequent evaluation branches return the corresponding letter grade as soon as the threshold condition matches[cite: 9]. Once a `return` statement executes, the JVM immediately terminates the method call frame, so no subsequent conditions are evaluated[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Validate score bounds (`score < 0 || score > 100`) as the first guard clause[cite: 7, 9].
Order conditional returns from highest threshold to lowest: `>= 90`, `>= 80`, `>= 70`, `>= 60`[cite: 7, 9].
Return immediately on each branch without nesting `else` statements[cite: 9].

Score 82: B
Score 55: F
Score 105: INVALID

questions.title: Recursive Digit Summation
questions.question: Write a recursive method `sumDigits(int n)` that sums the digits of an integer by peeling off digits using `% 10` and recursing on `/ 10`[cite: 7, 9, 11].
questions.explanation: Recursive method evaluation breaks a problem down by having a method call itself with smaller inputs until reaching a base condition[cite: 6, 9]. In `sumDigits(int n)`, the rightmost digit is isolated using the modulus operator (`Math.abs(n) % 10`), while the remaining prefix is extracted via integer division (`Math.abs(n) / 10`)[cite: 7, 9]. The base condition occurs when $n < 10$, where the method returns the single digit directly[cite: 6, 9]. For larger numbers, it returns `(n % 10) + sumDigits(n / 10)`[cite: 7, 9]. Each recursive step pushes a stack frame; once the base case is reached, the frames unwind and sum the values back to the original caller[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Normalize negative numbers using `Math.abs(n)` to handle negative inputs correctly[cite: 7, 9].
Base case: `if (n < 10) return n;` terminates the recursion[cite: 6, 9].
Recursive step: `return (n % 10) + sumDigits(n / 10);`[cite: 7, 9].

questions.title: Defensive Copying vs Unmodifiable Collections
questions.question: Demonstrate how returning a private mutable collection directly from a getter leaks internal state, and fix the issue using `Collections.unmodifiableList()` or defensive copying[cite: 10, 11].
questions.explanation: Returning direct heap references to private mutable objects compromises encapsulation[cite: 5, 10]. If a getter returns an internal `ArrayList` reference directly (`return this.roles;`), external callers can invoke `.clear()` or `.add()` on it, mutating internal class state without validation[cite: 5, 10]. To protect encapsulation, methods should return either a defensive copy (`new ArrayList<>(this.roles)`) or an unmodifiable view via `Collections.unmodifiableList(this.roles)`[cite: 10]. Any attempt to modify an unmodifiable view throws an `UnsupportedOperationException`, preventing external callers from altering internal state[cite: 10].
hints: Show the vulnerability by modifying the list returned from the vulnerable getter[cite: 10].
Implement a secure getter using `Collections.unmodifiableList(roles)` or `List.copyOf(roles)`[cite: 10].
Catch `UnsupportedOperationException` to confirm that the unmodifiable view blocks external modifications[cite: 10].
questions.expectedOutput:
Modification blocked by unmodifiable view!
Internal permissions preserved: [READ, WRITE]

questions.title: Higher-Order Function Factory via Method Return
questions.question: Write a factory method `makeMultiplier(int factor)` that returns a `Function<Integer, Integer>` lambda, and use it to instantiate reusable multiplier functions[cite: 11].
questions.explanation: In functional programming with Java 8+, methods can treat functions as first-class citizens: accepting them as arguments or returning them as return values[cite: 1, 9]. The `makeMultiplier(int factor)` method returns a `java.util.function.Function<Integer, Integer>` instance implemented via a lambda expression: `x -> x * factor`[cite: 1]. The returned lambda captures the local parameter `factor` from its enclosing method scope[cite: 6]. Because `factor` is effectively final, it remains available within the lambda's closure long after `makeMultiplier` has finished executing[cite: 6]. This demonstrates higher-order functions, closures, and functional composition in modern Java[cite: 1].
hints: Specify the return type as `Function<Integer, Integer>` using `java.util.function.Function`[cite: 1, 9].
Return a lambda expression capturing the parameter: `return x -> x * factor;`[cite: 1, 6].
Invoke the returned function using the `.apply(value)` method[cite: 1].
